transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-14 15:00 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Marcus Hale (Redwood AE), Priya Ramaswamy (Redwood SE), Jenna Ortiz (CEO, Obsidian Labs), Marco Silva (CTO), Riley Chen (SRE)

Summary/Context note: Obsidian is building real-time code-assist for internal developer tools. They currently use a mix of cloud model APIs and a small internal Triton cluster for latency-sensitive routes. Primary constraint is monthly inference budget and predictable latency for paid customers. They want to understand unit economics and when to move to Dedicated or Private.

00:00 Marcus (AE): Okay everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros then we'll jump into your workload and budget. Marcus here, AE on Redwood. Priya from SE will cover technical levers.
00:18 Jenna (CEO): Hi, thanks, yes quick intros — we're excited to see the cost side. We're trying to figure out if hosted gives us enough predictability or whether we need dedicated.
00:27 Marco (CTO): Right, we have some endpoints that need sub-100ms p95 for certain flows, and others where latency can be 500-800ms. Budget is... kind of tight, we have a $30k/month cap for inference initially.
00:45 Priya (SE): Thanks. Can you share typical prompt lengths and QPS? That helps with batching and cache sizing.
:55 Riley (SRE): Average prompt about 75 tokens, responses 150 tokens. Peak concurrent requests around 120 QPS for some internal events. Normal steady-state ~20 QPS.
01:12 Marcus: Great — that's really helpful. High-level: our per-token hosted pricing is X (we shared a pricing page), but unit cost moves based on effective batching, kv cache hits, and quantized model choice. We can run scenarios for your 75/150 distribution.
01:35 Jenna: When you say "kv cache hits" — does that work for code context? We have a lot of reuse across calls, like bringing in repo context.
01:45 Priya: Yes, prefix/KV caching is often very effective for code-assist. If many requests reuse the same context tokens, the runtime serves them from cache and you only pay for new decode tokens effectively. In practice we see 20-70% token reduction for heavy reuse patterns, but results vary.
02:10 Marco: Is that automatic or do we need to change our prompts?
02:16 Priya: It's mostly automatic if the context is the same. You can also pin prefixes or use session tokens. We'll send example configs.
02:28 Riley: If we get 50% token reduction from caching that would double our runway. But how does that interplay with batching and latency?
02:38 Priya: Good question. Batching increases throughput but adds latency while waiting to collect a batch. For your sub-100ms p95 routes, batching window would be minimal, so less batching. For 500ms routes you can tune larger windows and get much lower per-token cost.
02:59 Marcus: So the tradeoff is, for p95 < 100ms we recommend Dedicated with pinned capacity or even private for on-prem if you have residency needs. Hosted can still be used with burst capacity but it's typically pricier per-token if you need low latency and low batching.
03:20 Marco: Can you quantify — ballpark per-token numbers across hosting modes?
03:27 Marcus: Without getting too deep here, for a model like a 13B quantized we usually see hosted effective cost per 1k tokens around $Y with no caching and modest batching. With dedicated it's often 20-40% cheaper at scale, private slightly cheaper or similar depending on infra costs and util. But we'll run exact numbers against your QPS and profiles.
03:48 Jenna: You're saying Dedicated gives both latency predictability and lower cost?
03:54 Marcus: Predictability yes — because you reserve capacity. Cost depends on utilization; if you underutilize the reserved GPUs cost per token goes up. That's why we look at modes: bursty steady vs constant high QPS.
04:10 Riley: We have bursty spikes tied to nightly CI runs and midday internal demos. How does burst capacity work?
04:18 Priya: We offer burst pools that can be configured to kick in — there are tradeoffs and a small premium for burst. You can model that as a blended unit price.
04:30 Marco: I heard something about routing by policy — can we route non-sensitive traffic to hosted and sensitive to private?
04:36 Marcus: Absolutely. Smart routing can split by sensitivity, SLO, or cost. Many customers use hosted for low-sensitivity and private/VPC for regulated traffic.
04:47 Jenna: On compliance — we need SOC2 and KMS integration. Any concerns for private?
04:52 Priya: Private/VPC supports customer-managed KMS/HSM and you get audit logs. For hosted we have SOC2 and you can request dedicated logging retention options. We'll share the SOC2 report and the private deployment checklist.
05:06 Marco: What about live keys, SSO, RBAC?
05:12 Marcus: SSO and SAML are supported for the console, RBAC for team roles, and key rotation via KMS. We'll send the docs.
05:20 Riley: Back to numbers — can you show a sensitivity table: per-token cost vs batch size vs cache hit rate?
05:27 Priya: Yes, we'll produce a matrix. Quick heuristic: doubling average batch size roughly halves per-token decode cost up to GPU saturation limits. Caching reduces input tokens billed. Also quantization reduces GPU cycles per token which reduces cost.
06:00 Jenna: About quantization — how big is the tradeoff in quality for code completion? We can't accept hallucinations.
06:08 Priya: For code workloads, 4-bit quantization often works well for most 13B/34B families, but we recommend evals. Redwood Optimize can run quality regressions tied to your prompt set. That's part of our pilot offer.
06:26 Marcus: For the pilot: we propose a 2-week hosted pilot with your traffic replay (redacted PII), we'll instrument caching and batching and show the delta in cost and latency. If the numbers look good we scope Dedicated sizing.
06:40 Marco: Sounds good. How do you measure effective hit rate for KV cache during the pilot?
06:46 Priya: We'll use token-level telemetry in the console and show cache-hit percentages and per-route token breakdown. There's tracing hooks per request.
06:58 Riley: Do you expose a sample of the telemetry? We need something our SREs can ingest.
07:03 Marcus: Yes, we provide logs and a metrics export (Prometheus style) and can push to your tenant.
07:12 Jenna: Competitors — we've been talking to Anthropic and evaluating an in-house Triton stack. How do you compare on cost predictability vs Anthropic?
07:23 Marcus: Anthropic's managed offering is comparable in simplicity; difference is we emphasize deterministic serving levers (kv cache, batching knobs) and dedicated/private abstractions. Self-hosted Triton gives control but raises ops cost — which you have today. We'll show a cost/ops tradeoff.
07:44 Marco: Ops cost question — if we go private, do we own the infra maintenance?
07:48 Priya: For Private on-prem we provide the control plane and deployment artifacts; ops still manage hardware but Redwood supports upgrades and runtime tweaks as part of the enterprise agreement.
07:58 Riley: SLA questions — what uptime and latency SLAs for Dedicated?
08:03 Marcus: We offer a 99.9% uptime SLA for Dedicated plus latency targets depending on committed capacity; we can include SLO objectives in the contract.
08:14 Jenna: Any hidden costs — egress, logs, telemetry?
08:18 Marcus: Telemetry and basic logs are included; extended retention and high-fidelity traces are add-ons. Egress is standard cloud egress if you host in your VPC. We'll call out line items in the proposal.
08:30 Marco: Ok let's try the pilot. What do you need from us to size the pilot?
08:34 Priya: A week of traffic replay or a synthetic script that matches peak and steady-state QPS, your sample prompt set, and the list of routes that require sub-100ms. Also permission to enable prefix caching instrumentation.
08:47 Jenna: We can provide that. Also want an ROI snapshot for three months showing hosted vs dedicated vs private.
08:52 Marcus: We'll produce a three-month runway model with sensitivity to cache hit rate and batch windows.
08:58 Riley: Any recommended quick wins?
09:02 Priya: Start by enabling prefix caching for session-based flows, tune batching windows differently for real-time vs background routes, and try a smaller quantized model for background tasks.
09:14 Marcus: We'll email sample configs.
09:20 Jenna: Great. Recap and next steps?
09:23 Marcus: Recap: Redwood will send cost model spreadsheet, SOC2 and private deploy checklist, KV cache config examples, and a pilot plan. Obsidian will share traffic replay, prompt samples, and SLO list. Schedule a 60-min technical deep-dive for next week.
09:38 Marco: That works.
09:41 Jenna: Thanks all.
09:42 Marcus: Thanks — we'll follow up.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcription contains minor mis-hearings; timestamps approximate. Links referenced during call: pricing page (link), SOC2.pdf (link), KU_cache_config_examples.md (link), cost-model.xlsx (link).
